Diocletian. A Roman emperor who ruled from AD 284 to 305. Coming to power at a time of chaos in the Crisis of the Third Century, he fundamentally reorganised the empire's administration and military. To manage the vast and embattled Roman state, he instituted the Tetrarchy, dividing power among four co-emperors, and eventually became the first Roman emperor to voluntarily abdicate the throne.

He established the Tetrarchy, or rule of four, splitting the empire into Eastern and Western halves, each governed by an Augustus as senior emperor and a Caesar as junior emperor. He initiated the Diocletianic Persecution, the empire's last, largest, and bloodiest official persecution of Christianity. He attempted to curb massive inflation by issuing the Edict on Maximum Prices, which fixed prices for goods and services but proved largely unenforceable. He voluntarily retired to a massive, heavily fortified palace in Spalatum, which is modern-day Split in Croatia, where he grew cabbages. After his abdication, the Tetrarchic system quickly collapsed into a series of civil wars among the remaining leaders and their sons.

Maximian was his trusted general and appointed co-emperor, serving as Augustus of the West during the Tetrarchy. Constantine the Great was the future emperor who eventually emerged from the collapse of the Tetrarchy to reunite the empire.
